questions.q: The tasks part of the app wants the notifications part to send a reminder, and it needs to know whether that worked. Which fits?
questions.explain: Events tell ("this happened") and ignore handler results. Messages ask ("please do this, and tell me how it went"), and the handler's return value comes back to the sender.
options: An event, because events always return answers
A message: it asks for something and brings the answer back
An event with the THROW error mode

questions.q: Which is a typical message type name?
questions.explain: A message is an instruction, like reminder.send. The past-tense names announce something that already happened, which makes them events.

questions.q: Why send a message instead of importing the notifications code and calling it directly?
questions.explain: A direct call is fine while the app is small. A message keeps the two parts apart: they only agree on a type and a payload shape. Both are still in-process and can be lost in a crash.
options: Messages are always faster than function calls
As the app grows into modules, every module importing every other module turns into a tangle; with a message, sender and handler only share the type name
Imports do not work between folders
Messages are saved to disk, so they are never lost

questions.q: What happens when a handler fails, for events compared with messages?
questions.explain: Event handlers are independent reactions, so one failure does not stop the others. A message asks for one job, so the first failure ends the dispatch with success: false.
options: Both stop at once and throw
Both keep running the other handlers
Events keep running the other handlers; a message dispatch stops and reports the failure

questions.q: Why give every message handler an id?
questions.explain: An error like Handler "send-reminder" failed: ... tells you exactly where to look, and bus.off("send-reminder") removes that handler.
options: The bus refuses handlers without one
Errors can name the handler that failed, and you can remove it later with bus.off(id)

questions.q: What does a branded id like the result of toCorrelationId("req-7f3a") give you?
questions.explain: The brand only exists for the type checker. You brand a string once, and toCorrelationId also rejects empty strings.
options: An encrypted string that nobody can read
An object with extra methods at runtime
At runtime it is a plain string, but TypeScript will not accept any old string there, so you cannot pass a user id by mistake
A number that is faster to compare

questions.q: A handler throws. Why does bus.send return { success: false, error } instead of throwing?
questions.explain: Every caller gets a result and checks result.success. The failure is in result.error, wrapped in a MessageHandlerError that names the handler.
options: Because the error is hidden from you on purpose
It forces you to look at the outcome instead of forgetting a try
Because JavaScript cannot throw from async functions
Because the handler is retried automatically

questions.q: You send reminder.snd (a typo) and nobody handles it. The result says success: true. How do you catch this kind of mistake for a request that needs an answer?
questions.explain: The bus cannot tell "nobody needed to answer" from "you misspelled the address". Checking hasHandlers when the app starts turns the typo into an immediate failure instead of a silent success.
options: Create the bus with allowMultipleHandlers: false and check bus.hasHandlers(type) at start-up
Give the message a longer timeout

questions.q: With allowMultipleHandlers: false, what happens when code registers a second handler for reminder.send?
questions.explain: A second handler for a request is a bug. Failing at registration time, at start-up, is much better than a surprise in production.
options: The second handler silently replaces the first
Both run, and value becomes an array
bus.on throws at once, so the mistake fails when the app starts
The second handler is ignored without an error

questions.q: In @zudojs/messaging, in which order does middleware run?
questions.explain: Here 10 runs before 20. That is the opposite of the event bus, so always look it up for the package you use.
options: Highest priority number first, like the event bus
Ascending: the lowest priority number first, and the default is 100
In the order the messages were sent

questions.q: Why validate message payloads in middleware?
questions.explain: Validating in the handler is fine too. In middleware, every dispatch is checked, so a handler never runs with bad data.
options: No handler can forget the check, and a payload often came from outside (an HTTP body, a queue), so it is untrusted input
Because middleware runs after the handler
Because validation in handlers is not allowed

questions.q: What is a correlation id?
questions.explain: Every message in the chain carries the same correlation id, so one search in the logs finds the whole story. The direct parent is the causation id.
options: The id of the one message that directly caused this one
An id shared by everything that belongs to one bigger operation, usually one HTTP request
A random id created for each handler

questions.q: What is a causation id for?
questions.explain: createDerivedMessage(parent, input) keeps the parent's correlation id and records the parent's id as the cause of the new message.
options: Grouping all messages from one request
Naming the one message that directly caused this one, so you can rebuild the chain step by step

questions.q: In the Task API, what should you use as the correlation id?
questions.explain: The observability lesson puts the same request id on every log line and trace, so one search finds everything that happened for one request.
options: A new random id for each message

questions.q: A dispatch times out after 45 ms. What happens to the handler that is still running?
questions.explain: JavaScript cannot kill a running function. The caller gets a MessageTimeoutError at once, and the signal is aborted; a handler that ignores the signal keeps wasting resources.
options: It keeps running until it checks context.signal and stops itself
It is restarted from the beginning
Its result is still returned to the caller

questions.q: A handler calls an outside service with fetch. How does it make the request stop when the dispatch is cancelled?
questions.explain: An AbortSignal is the standard "stop, nobody needs this any more" object, and many built-in functions accept it. fetch cancels the request itself when the signal aborts.

questions.q: The caller aborts its AbortController. The only handler notices the abort and simply returns "cancelled". What does the caller see?
questions.explain: An aborted dispatch is reported as aborted even when the handler returns normally (since @zudojs/messaging 1.2.0), so the caller can never mistake cancelled work for finished work. send only throws when the signal was already aborted before the dispatch started.
options: success: true with the value "cancelled", so the caller believes the work was done

questions.q: The reminder handler fails. What should the route send to the client?
questions.explain: Internal error details can leak how your system works. Log the real reason, and give the client a short message that is safe to show.
options: The full error with the stack trace, to help the user
A short, safe message like 502 Could not send the reminder; the real reason goes to the logs

questions.q: The reminder is sent while the user waits for the response. What is the weakness, and what fixes it?
questions.explain: An in-process message lives in memory while the request runs. The background jobs lesson moves this work onto a queue, which survives crashes and retries on its own.
options: Messages are too slow; use events instead
A slow mail server makes the request slow and a crash loses the reminder; a queue fixes both
Nothing, in-process messages are never lost
The correlation id is lost; use a causation id

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: send resolves after the handler has finished, and value is what the handler returned.
options:
sending for task 1
true { delivered: true }

true { delivered: true }
sending for task 1

sending for task 1
true [ { delivered: true } ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A failing handler does not make send throw. The result has success: false and a MessageHandlerError that names the handler.
options: An uncaught Error: mail server is down

false true
Handler "send-reminder" failed: mail server is down

false false
mail server is down

true true
Handler "send-reminder" failed: mail server is down

questions.q: Nobody handles this type. What does this print?
questions.explain: A message that nobody handles still counts as a success, with an empty list as its value. That is why requests need hasHandlers checks at start-up.

questions.q: Several handlers are allowed (the default). What does this print?
questions.explain: With several handlers, they run one after another, lowest priority number first, and value is an array of their results.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first handler that fails stops the rest, so cleanup never runs and there is no value. That is the difference from the event bus, which keeps going.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With allowMultipleHandlers: false, a second handler for the same type throws at once. hasHandlers then tells you which types are covered.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Like an event, a message is a frozen object with an id, a type, a payload and a timestamp, plus optional source and correlationId.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A branded id is a plain string at runtime. The brand only exists for TypeScript. Empty strings are rejected.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The follow-up keeps the parent's correlation id and records the parent's id as its cause. It still gets its own new id.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Message middleware runs in ascending priority order: 5, then 50, then the default 100. The event bus does the opposite.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: When a middleware throws, the result is success: false and error is exactly what it threw. The handler never ran with bad data.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: After 20 ms, send returns a timeout failure and the caller moves on. The handler was not stopped by force: it kept running, and when it woke up it saw that its signal was aborted.
options:
handler noticed the abort
false true

false true
handler noticed the abort

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The signal was already aborted, so the dispatch never started. That is one of the few cases where send throws instead of returning a result.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: bus.dispose() releases the bus when the app shuts down. After that, every send throws.

questions.q: Register a handler for tax.calculate with the id calculate-tax. It returns the tax: amount * rate from the payload. Then send one message with amount: 200 and rate: 0.2, and keep the result in result.
questions.explain: bus.on(type, handler, { id }) registers, and bus.send({ type, payload }) returns { success, value, error }. The handler's return value arrives in value.

questions.q: Finish remind(taskId). Send reminder.send with { taskId }. If the result is not a success, return { status: 502, body: { error: "Could not send the reminder" } }. Otherwise return { status: 202, body: result.value }. Never put the real error in the body.
questions.explain: send does not throw when the handler fails, so check result.success. The real reason (here an internal address) belongs in your logs, not in the client's response.
questions.expected:
{ status: 202, body: { delivered: true } }
{ status: 502, body: { error: 'Could not send the reminder' } }

questions.q: Create the bus so a message type may have only one handler. The second bus.on must then throw, and the program prints the error's name.
questions.explain: With allowMultipleHandlers: false, the value is the one handler's answer instead of an array, and a second handler fails at start-up.

questions.q: At start-up, check that every type in required has a handler. Print missing handler: <type> for each one without a handler, then print ready only when none is missing.
questions.explain: A message nobody handles still "succeeds", so a missing handler would go unnoticed. bus.hasHandlers(type) at start-up turns it into a clear failure.
questions.expected:
missing handler: reminder.cancel
missing handler: report.build

questions.q: Add a middleware with bus.use that prints -> <type> before next() and <- <type> after it, even when an inner layer throws. Use try/finally and return the result of next().
questions.explain: finally runs whether next() returned or threw, so the closing line always prints. Write return await next() so the error is caught inside the try.

questions.q: Add a middleware that checks reminder.send payloads: taskId must be a positive whole number. If not, throw new MessageValidationError("Invalid reminder.send payload"). Other message types pass straight through.
questions.explain: The check runs before any handler, so bad data never reaches one. Number.isInteger("1") is false, so the string is refused too. Always return next() for messages that pass.
questions.expected:
sent
Invalid reminder.send payload
Invalid reminder.send payload
3

questions.q: In the reminder.send handler, build a follow-up email.deliver message with createDerivedMessage (payload { to: "ada@example.com" }), dispatch it with bus.dispatch, and return its value.
questions.explain: createDerivedMessage copies the parent's correlation id and records the parent as the cause, so both handlers log the same id. bus.dispatch sends a message you already built.
questions.expected:
[req-7f3a] reminder.send
[req-7f3a] email.deliver to ada@example.com
result: queued

questions.q: Finish buildReport(signal): for pages 1 to 5, call signal.throwIfAborted() first, then wait 20 ms and print built page <n>. Return "report ready" at the end. The controller aborts after 30 ms with a reason.
questions.explain: An AbortController owns the signal and abort(reason) cancels it. throwIfAborted() does nothing until then, and afterwards throws the reason, so the work stops and is reported as cancelled. Message handlers use context.signal the same way.
questions.expected:
built page 1
built page 2
stopped: the user closed the page

questions.q: The handler checks its signal before each 30 ms page, and the dispatch has a 45 ms timeout. What does this print?
questions.explain: The timeout came while page 2 was being built. The handler finished that page, then throwIfAborted() threw before page 3. Without the check it would have built all 5 pages for nobody.

questions.q: Write a middleware that counts failed dispatches in failures. Catch the error from next(), add 1, and re-throw it so the result still reports the failure.
questions.explain: A handler's error reaches the middleware as a thrown error. If the middleware swallowed it, the dispatch would look like a success; re-throwing keeps the result honest.
